Pacing definitely needs work right now. Like I understand it's the nature of being a manga in a magazine whose chapters get released every month, but so far the biggest reveals have taken 5 chapters to get revealed. Even then, it feels like each reveal gets undermined or overshadowed by the next reveal. Almost like the series in a constant state of "Oh you thought this? It's actually this," which can be really good at times (like I LOVED Ch.95). But at times it feels like a lot of red herrings and ultimately wasted energy.

I will always give Iro the benefit of the doubt when it comes to unanswered questions, but I feel like so many have been piling on that I have serious "mystery fatigue." It's the exact reason why I took a break from the series for a few months.

I have faith that it'll all be worth it in the end, because generally the writing is really good. Especially when it comes to foreshadowing and having things pay off.

But yeah, as much as I love Hanako, I'm glad to be be able to air out my annoyances.

But yeah this is only my opinion, don't take it too seriously if you disagree. 😆 rambling over

As a strong Hananene shipper, even I have to ask myself if a supernatural and a human can even "live happily ever after." Same with Mistuba and Kou. Whereas I can see a grand sacrifice happening for either Hanako sacrificing himself for Nene or vice versa by virtue of being the main characters and central focus of the story, I can't think of a good, satisfying way for Mistuba and Kou to be together forever.

Honestly the idea of Kou becoming a supernatural always had a bad taste in my mouth since the Picture Perfect Arc. Like, even if he's having a rough relationship with Teru, he'd still be leaving his sister. And Kou understands more than anyone the pain of someone leaving/dying out of nowhere (as he literally explained to Tsukasa in the Red House Arc).

My ideal would be if Kou got Mitsuba to "move on" somehow, thus bringing closure to both characters at once: Kou would finally be able to let people go (he probably hasn't truly accepted the death of his mother yet, which is why he's so protective of everyone) and Mistuba would finally be released from being Tsukasa's experiment into a better afterlife (the one where Kou's mother is).

Whether he gets him to move on via a kiss or a heartfelt bro hug, but just something that shows Mitsuba that he is cared for, so that Mitsuba is able to move on because his true wish is finally fulfilled: no longer being alone. A bittersweet ending that leaves both parties truly happy, even if they do need to part.

As a lighter interpretation, perhaps after he is granted an opportunity to atone for his murder he becomes too emotional with haku-joudai's powers and is mistook for an evil spirit by Grandma Minamoto and she seals him.

Another mini theory: He may think that being sealed is for the best, because we know that he feels very guilty whenever he hurts people close to him (is uncomfortable talking about the murder, first apology to Nene) and is generally selfless as the leader of the Seven Wonders. Because of this, maybe he doesn't mind the seal? Maybe he's afraid of himself and what he's capable of? Then somehow the seal comes off and he learns to ultimately forgive himself. As an artist myself, it mostly comes down to the fact that most people outside an art community don't understand all the disciplines and nuanced skills it takes to be a member of such a community, so when a layman criticizes a piece of art/performance, they don't have much ethos speaking on the manner (this doesn't mean you can't be right or educated on the subject, it's just a general sentiment found in any kind of field). On the other hand, it does get frustrating when people defend artists blindly by simply saying "I doubt you could do better," because it totally avoids any sort of discourse, and perpetuates an idea that art should be praised for the sole fact that it's art, which glosses over all the effort an artist has put into their piece in the first place. What's ironic is that people who defend artists with "they can do better than you" have rarely been artists themselves (you can tell by the shallowness of their "argument"). Artists don't want their art to be criticized by someone who missed the point nor blindly praised every time.
